name: The Shear Line
observation:
The six tumbler drums (InstancedMesh on the shaft at x=2.8, z=-2.5..+2.5, read-slots at y=1.45) are re-timed to step TOGETHER — the whole bank clicks one detent at a time instead of six drums drifting at six rates. Each drum carries a different fixed glyph offset, so at any instant the row shows six DIFFERENT engraved marks out of the eight faces, and exactly two of the eight faces are out of the bank. Which two are out rotates with every click.

The eight bolt collars around the blast door are re-stencilled so each carries one of those same eight engraved marks (reusing the file's existing drawGlyph()), plus its room code and a two-digit number. Two collars are struck through in bolt-blue — those bolts are THROWN.

The tell the player actually watches is the six bolt-blue backlight bars already sitting under the read-slots. Each bar lights only while its drum is showing a glyph that appears on a LIVE (unstruck) collar. So the row of bars visibly changes pattern on every click: five frames of the cycle have two bars dark, two frames have one dark, and exactly ONE frame per cycle has all six lit. Verified over 200,000 seeds — the 1/2/5 profile and the uniqueness of the all-lit frame are structural, not lucky.

At that all-lit frame the bank also DWELLS for a double beat (5.0s instead of 2.5s) while the amber ceiling beacon, re-phased to a strict 2.5s metronome, keeps beating. The beacon strikes nine times per cycle; the bank only moves eight. The seating is therefore visible twice over: the bars all go blue, and the bank pauses.
deduction:
"Bolt-blue means SEATED" is already the room's stencilled colour law. The rule the player has to notice is that the backlights are not decoration and not random — a tumbler can only seat on a bolt that is still live, so a drum showing one of the two struck-through glyphs stays dark. Once that clicks, the whole bank going blue at once stops being a pretty flash and becomes a statement: at this instant NEITHER thrown bolt is anywhere in the stack. That is the shear line. That is the moment the safe would open.

The second half of the deduction is where the numbers live. Nothing on a drum is a number — the drums only carry shapes. The player has to work out that the shape is a pointer: each seated glyph names a collar on the door, and the collar carries the two-digit number. So the answer has to be assembled by turning round, matching six engraved marks against the ring of eight stencils, and reading numbers off the door.

The closing satisfaction is that the two halves confirm each other. At the seated frame the six drums show precisely the six live collars — the complement of the two struck ones. A player who has done it right can check their own work: the six numbers they collected should be exactly the six collar numbers that are not crossed out. Nothing tells them this; it just turns out to be true, which is the "oh, THAT's what's happening" landing twice.

The deliberate anti-shortcut: brute force exists but is strictly dominated. A player holding the key but refusing to find the seated frame faces eight candidate answers — but generating all eight means doing the glyph-to-collar mapping 48 times, which is far more work than watching one 22.5s cycle. The lazy path is harder than the intended path.
answerFormat: 6 digits (three two-digit collar numbers, concatenated). Digits only — no letters, so no I/1 or O/0 confusion — and the generator draws collar numbers from 11-99 using digits 1-9 only, so a spoken zero can never be misheard as a letter. Spoken as pairs: "one nine, seven three, two seven."
neighbourKeyRole:
The key is a READING RULE, never a value that appears in the answer. It reads: "SLOT 4 / TOWARD THE PANELS" — a starting slot (1-6) and a direction along the shaft. Slots number 1 at the panel end to 6 at the door end; you read three slots from the start point in the named direction, continuing round the shaft if you run off an end.

This gates ordering and selection only. The holder next door has never seen the Vault, has no glyph-to-collar mapping and no idea when the bank seats, so the string is inert in their hands — they are holding a sentence about furniture they cannot see. The Vault player, conversely, can do every scrap of the real thinking without it: find the seated frame, map all six glyphs, collect all six numbers — and still be stuck, because six numbers in slot order is not the answer and there are 12 start/direction combinations (6 starts x 2 directions). At LOCKOUT_MS = 30s per wrong answer that is up to six minutes of penalty, so guessing is unattractive but the player is never helpless-and-idle: there is genuine work to fill the wait for their neighbour, and genuine work left after the call connects.

Crucially the key cannot be pre-collected and banked, because it is useless until the Vault player has already deduced the mapping — it is the last piece, not the first, which is the opposite of the current cipher-shift design.
seededValues: collarGlyph[0..7] — a shuffled bijection assigning the eight drawGlyph kinds to the eight collar ring positions, so the shape-to-collar mapping is different every session
collarNum[0..7] — eight distinct two-digit numbers drawn from digits 1-9 only (no zero, so nothing can be misheard as the letter O)
collarCode[0..7] — the two-letter room codes shuffled across the ring (flavour; keeps the cross-room 'bolt register' fiction alive)
thrown — which TWO ring positions are struck through, rejected and redrawn if the two glyph kinds are 4 apart mod 8, since a gap of 4 produces a second seated frame and destroys uniqueness

fSeat — which of the eight frames is the seated one, chosen uniformly 0-7; the two absent drum offsets are then derived as (G-fSeat) mod 8 so the seating is exact by construction rather than by search
drumOffset[0..5] — a shuffle of the six remaining glyph kinds across the six slots, which fixes the whole visible pattern
cycleOffsetSeconds — a real-valued phase in [0, 22.5) so the first seating does not land at the same wall-clock moment every session
keyStart (1-6) and keyDir (toward the door / toward the panels) — the neighbour's key, regenerated by the existing ring repair pass if it ever collides

geometryChanges.change: Collar stencil atlas (makeCollarAtlas): redraw each cell as engraved shape mark + two-digit number + small dim room code, calling the file's EXISTING drawGlyph(ctx, kind) at r=34 for the mark. Atlas grows 512x256 -> 768x384 (192px cells) and the stencil quads grow 0.20m -> 0.28m so three elements stay legible from across a 6.6m room. The quads already sit at COLLAR_Z-0.05, in front of the bolt heads, so enlarging them occludes nothing.
geometryChanges.cost: Zero new draw calls — same single atlas, same single makeAtlasQuads mesh, same material. Texture memory 0.5MB -> 1.1MB. No new geometry.

geometryChanges.change: Collar numbers, room codes, glyph assignment and which two are struck through all become server-seeded instead of the hardcoded BOLT_REGISTER const. NOTE: the existing comment warns these are 'fixed strings, not seeded' because another room reads them aloud — that reasoning still holds and is satisfied, because the seed is per-SESSION and shared by every client in every chamber, so all clients still agree. What must be checked is that no other room's puzzle assumes the literal old values ('EN 08', 'VE 05').
geometryChanges.cost: None — same canvas pass, same draw call. Requires seed plumbing (see below).

geometryChanges.change: Per-drum backlight state: remap the UVs of each of the six merged backlight bars to sample texel i of a new 6x1 RGBA DataTexture (NearestFilter), and hang that texture on the existing backlightMaterial as emissiveMap. The material keeps emissive=BOLT_BLUE, so the texture simply gates each bar on or off. All six verts of a bar get u=(i+0.5)/6, v=0.5 — a single texel per bar, immune to filtering seams.
geometryChanges.cost: Zero new draw calls, zero new materials, zero new lights, zero new geometry. A 24-byte texture upload, and only when the frame index actually changes (once per 2.5s), not per frame.

geometryChanges.change: Drum timing: delete the six-element drumPeriod/drumPhase arrays and the per-drum drumAngle() call. Replace with ONE bank clock computed once per update — eight steps of 2.5s with the seated step doubled to 5.0s, total cycle 22.5s — then seatDrum(i, (step + ease + drumOffset[i]) * DETENT_STEP). Keep ease inside the frame and added BEFORE the multiply, so the 7->0 wrap passes through 8*45deg = 360deg and the drums never snap backwards.
geometryChanges.cost: Cheaper than the current code — one clock evaluation per frame instead of six, and an 8-iteration table walk that is trivially deterministic from elapsed + seed.

geometryChanges.change: Dwell tuning: raise the CLICK constant from 0.78 to 0.86. Ordinary frames hold still for 2.15s and click over in 0.35s; the seated frame holds still for 4.3s. A 0.35s move through 45deg still reads unmistakably as indexed detent motion, never as the Engine Room's smooth spin.

Beacon: re-phase from the free-running 1.6 rad/s to a strict 2.5s metronome locked to the step boundaries (omega = 2pi/2.5), peaking exactly on each click. Because 22.5 = 9 x 2.5 the lock holds across the whole cycle, which is what produces the 'nine beats, eight moves' tell.
geometryChanges.cost: Re-times existing — the beacon light and dome material are already driven every frame in update().

geometryChanges.change: drumLight (the existing bolt-blue point light at DRUM_X-0.6) scales with the number of seated tumblers: intensity = settings.drumLight * (0.55 + 0.45 * litCount/6). The seating frame washes the whole room blue for a beat.
geometryChanges.cost: Zero — reuses one of the room's four existing lights. No fifth light, which the file's header notes is what tanked the first draft.

geometryChanges.change: Seed plumbing: the server must pass the derived room config (collar table, drum offsets, fSeat, cycleOffset) to createVault(). No seed is currently threaded from server to room module anywhere in the codebase — this is the one piece of genuinely new wiring the design needs, and it is shared infrastructure every reworked chamber will want.
geometryChanges.cost: No render cost. Touches server/puzzles.js, the join payload, and the createVault() signature.

fragmentBrief:
TUMBLER BANK — 6 SLOTS, 8 FACES

The bank steps together. The beacon keeps the beat.
Eight faces, six slots: two faces are always out of the bank.

BOLT REGISTER
A collar struck through in blue is a THROWN bolt.
Bolt-blue is never information in this room. It means SEATED.

Slots number 1 at the panel end to 6 at the door end.
Read on round the shaft if you run off an end.

Your neighbour holds where to start and which way to read.
Six digits. No spaces.

[canvas diagram: a row of six numbered slot rectangles, "PANELS" labelled at the left end and "DOOR" at the right, with a small legend below showing a lit bar beside a dark bar — the convention only, no values]

Deliberately absent: any statement that the seated moment exists, that all six bars light at once, that the bank dwells, or that the numbers come off the collars. It points at the register, the colour law and the slot numbering the key depends on, and stops there.
exampleWalkthrough:
Session seed produces this collar ring (position: glyph, code, number):
  0: PLUS "VA 73"    1: SQUARE-DOT "EN 46" STRUCK    2: DOUBLE-BAR "AR 38"
  3: TRIANGLE "OB 91"    4: HOURGLASS "KC 27"    5: BOLT "SP 64" STRUCK
  6: DIAMOND "DC 52"    7: CHEVRONS "VE 19"
Thrown glyphs are SQUARE-DOT and BOLT (gap 7, not 4, so the seating is unique).
fSeat = 5. Absent offsets derive as 5 and 4, leaving drum offsets {0,1,2,3,6,7}, dealt to slots 1-6 as [3,7,0,6,1,2]. cycleOffset = 6.25s.

The player watches the bar row. "#" = lit, "." = dark:
  f=0  ####..     f=1  ##.#.#     f=2  #..###     f=3  #.#.##
  f=4  ###.##     f=5  ######     f=6  .#####     f=7  .####.
Frame 5 is the only full row, and it is the frame where the bank pauses for a double beat. Note frames 4 and 6 are one bar short — a careless glance can misread them, which is exactly the intended cost of not watching properly.

Timing: seated from elapsed 6.25s, still and readable until 10.55s, moving off at 11.25s, recurring every 22.5s (28.75s, 51.25s, ...).

At the seated frame the row reads, slot 1 (panel end) to slot 6 (door end):
  slot 1 TRIANGLE   -> collar OB 91
  slot 2 HOURGLASS  -> collar KC 27
  slot 3 PLUS       -> collar VA 73
  slot 4 CHEVRONS   -> collar VE 19
  slot 5 DIAMOND    -> collar DC 52
  slot 6 DOUBLE-BAR -> collar AR 38
Self-check the player can perform unprompted: {19,27,38,52,73,91} is exactly the set of collars NOT struck through. Confirmed identical in the verification run.

The neighbour reads out the key: "SLOT 4 / TOWARD THE PANELS."
Slots 4 -> 3 -> 2, so numbers 19, 73, 27.

ANSWER: 197327  — spoken "one nine, seven three, two seven."

Had the key instead been "SLOT 2 / TOWARD THE PANELS" the read would wrap round the shaft: slots 2 -> 1 -> 6, giving 279138. Same seated frame, same mapping, completely different answer — which is precisely the property that keeps the key load-bearing.
difficultyNotes:
Why a 13-year-old gets there: no arithmetic beyond concatenating three two-digit numbers, no cipher, no outside knowledge. Every step is shape-matching and reading. The room teaches its own rule — "BOLTS ENGAGED" is already stencilled on the north wall in bolt-blue and the file's own colour law says bolt-blue means engaged, so the backlights are a restatement of something the player has been looking at since they spawned. The all-lit frame is unmissable once you are watching the bars rather than the glyphs, and the double-beat dwell is a second, independent route to the same moment for a player who is counting beacon pulses instead of reading bars.

What stops it being instant: you cannot answer from a still frame. The room must be watched for at least one 22.5s cycle, and the read window is 4.3s inside it. The near-miss frames (`###.##`, `.#####`) mean a hurried player who grabs the first mostly-lit row gets a wrong answer and a 30s lockout, which is a cheap, fair, self-correcting lesson rather than a dead end. The glyph-to-collar mapping requires physically turning from the east wall drums to the south wall door and back, so the room gets used as a space instead of a screen. And even a player who has done all of that still cannot submit: three slots out of six, in one of two directions, is 12 orderings they have no way to pick between.

Sight lines check out: drums at y=1.45 against a 1.62m eye, collars spanning y=0.15 to y=2.25, everything under the 2.6m ceiling and nothing occluded — the collar stencils already sit proud of the bolt heads and the shaft hides behind the drums. Reading all six slots at once wants the player back near the west lattice (about 4.8m out, a 55-degree span, roughly 3 degrees per glyph), which is a nice incidental discovery: stand back to see the whole bank.

Two honest weak points, both deliberate. First, the all-lit flash is sufficient on its own — a player can find the moment without ever understanding WHY the bars are dark. I kept it rather than forcing them to spot the two absent glyphs unaided, because tracking a two-of-eight complement across 2.15s frames is beyond the stated age floor, and the real deduction work (glyph -> collar -> number) survives intact either way. Second, brute-forcing the eight frames is technically available; it is left in because it costs 48 mappings versus one cycle of watching, so it punishes itself without needing a rule against it.

One thing the builder must confirm against the actual mesh: whether the glyph seated in the read-slot at angle theta is (detent) mod 8 or (-detent) mod 8. That depends on the cylinder's UV wrap direction, and the sign is not derivable from reading the file. Get it backwards and every session generates a self-consistent but unsolvable room, since the deduced mapping would be mirrored. Verify it on screen with one hardcoded offset before wiring the seed in.
